"""
Exact numerical demonstration of the p-biased Fourier theory of the discrete cube
and of the two influence identities it yields.

Everything is computed in EXACT rational arithmetic (fractions.Fraction), so the
identities below are verified as literal equalities, not as floating-point
approximations.

Notation
--------
    V           a finite set of n sites; a configuration eta in {0,1}^V is stored
                as an integer bitmask, bit v set  <=>  site v is open.
    mu_p(eta)   = p^{#open} (1-p)^{#closed}          the p-biased product measure
    E_p[f]      = sum_eta mu_p(eta) f(eta)
    q           = p(1-p)                              the per-site variance
    psi_v(eta)  = 1-p if eta_v = 1, else -p           centred one-site character
    psi_S       = prod_{v in S} psi_v                 character of a set of sites
    fhat(S)     = E_p[f psi_S] / q^{|S|}              biased Fourier coefficient
    w_S(f)      = q^{|S|} fhat(S)^2                   energy at level S

Results demonstrated
--------------------
  * Product rule                E_p[prod_v g_v(eta_v)] = prod_v (p g_v(1) + (1-p) g_v(0))
  * Orthogonality               E_p[psi_S psi_T] = [S = T] q^{|S|}
  * Reproducing kernel          sum_S prod_{v in S} psi_v(xi)psi_v(eta)/q = [xi=eta]/mu_p(eta)
  * Completeness                f = sum_S fhat(S) psi_S
  * Parseval                    E_p[f g] = sum_S q^{|S|} fhat(S) ghat(S)
  * Plancherel (Boolean)        sum_S w_S(g_A) = 1
  * Energy decomposition        4P(1-P) = 4q sum_v I_v^2 + (energy at levels >= 2)
  * Site energy identity        sum_{S ni v} w_S(f) = q E_p[(D_v f)^2]   ( = 4 q I_v )
  * Efron-Stein / Poincare      q sum_v E_p[(D_v f)^2] - Var(f)
                                          = sum_{S != empty} (|S|-1) w_S(f) >= 0
  * Chaining identity           4q( sum_v I_v - sum_v I_v^2 ) = sum_{|S|>=2} |S| w_S(g_A)
  * Square-root law             ( sum_v I_v )^2 <= n P(1-P) / q
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Rat = Fraction


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Basic combinatorics of the cube                                            #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def popcount(mask: int) -> int:
    """Number of open sites in the configuration (or size of the set) `mask`."""
    return bin(mask).count("1")


def all_masks(n: int) -> range:
    """All 2^n configurations of an n-site cube, as bitmasks."""
    return range(1 << n)


def weight(p: Rat, eta: int, n: int) -> Rat:
    """mu_p(eta) = p^{#open} (1-p)^{#closed}."""
    k = popcount(eta)
    return p ** k * (1 - p) ** (n - k)


def expectation(p: Rat, table: Sequence[Rat], n: int) -> Rat:
    """E_p[f] for f given as a table indexed by configuration bitmask."""
    return sum(weight(p, eta, n) * table[eta] for eta in all_masks(n))


def psi(p: Rat, v: int, eta: int) -> Rat:
    """The centred one-site character psi_v(eta)."""
    return (1 - p) if (eta >> v) & 1 else -p


def psi_set(p: Rat, S: int, eta: int, n: int) -> Rat:
    """psi_S(eta) = prod_{v in S} psi_v(eta), with S a bitmask of sites."""
    out = Rat(1)
    for v in range(n):
        if (S >> v) & 1:
            out *= psi(p, v, eta)
    return out


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  The biased Fourier transform                                               #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def fourier_coefficients_direct(p: Rat, table: Sequence[Rat], n: int) -> List[Rat]:
    """Algorithm A: fhat(S) = E_p[f psi_S] / q^{|S|}, computed directly.

    Cost O(4^n n).  Used only as an independent cross-check of the fast method.
    """
    q = p * (1 - p)
    out: List[Rat] = []
    for S in all_masks(n):
        acc = Rat(0)
        for eta in all_masks(n):
            acc += weight(p, eta, n) * table[eta] * psi_set(p, S, eta, n)
        out.append(acc / q ** popcount(S))
    return out


def fourier_coefficients(p: Rat, table: Sequence[Rat], n: int) -> List[Rat]:
    """Algorithm B: the biased fast Walsh transform.  Cost O(n 2^n), exact.

    One pass per coordinate performs the one-coordinate decomposition
        f = A_v f + psi_v * D_v f,
        (A_v f)(eta) = p f(eta^{v->1}) + (1-p) f(eta^{v->0}),
        (D_v f)(eta) = f(eta^{v->1}) - f(eta^{v->0}),
    storing A_v f in the slot with bit v cleared and D_v f in the slot with bit v
    set.  Because the coefficients of f at sets avoiding v are those of A_v f, and
    at sets containing v are those of D_v f with v deleted, after n passes the
    entry indexed by the bitmask S is exactly fhat(S).
    """
    a = list(table)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for i in all_masks(n):
            if i & bit:
                continue
            hi, lo = a[i | bit], a[i]          # hi = value with v open
            a[i] = p * hi + (1 - p) * lo       # A_v f
            a[i | bit] = hi - lo               # D_v f
    return a


def level_energies(p: Rat, coeffs: Sequence[Rat], n: int) -> List[Rat]:
    """w_S(f) = q^{|S|} fhat(S)^2 for every level S."""
    q = p * (1 - p)
    return [q ** popcount(S) * coeffs[S] ** 2 for S in all_masks(n)]


def discrete_derivative(table: Sequence[Rat], v: int, n: int) -> List[Rat]:
    """(D_v f)(eta) = f(eta with v open) - f(eta with v closed)."""
    bit = 1 << v
    return [table[eta | bit] - table[eta & ~bit] for eta in all_masks(n)]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Events, influences, sign indicators                                        #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def sign_indicator(member: Callable[[int], bool], n: int) -> List[Rat]:
    """g_A = +1 on A, -1 off A, as a table."""
    return [Rat(1) if member(eta) else Rat(-1) for eta in all_masks(n)]


def event_probability(p: Rat, member: Callable[[int], bool], n: int) -> Rat:
    """P = mu_p(A)."""
    return sum(weight(p, eta, n) for eta in all_masks(n) if member(eta))


def influence(p: Rat, member: Callable[[int], bool], v: int, n: int) -> Rat:
    """I_v = mu_p{ eta : eta^{v->1} in A and eta^{v->0} not in A }."""
    bit = 1 << v
    total = Rat(0)
    for eta in all_masks(n):
        if member(eta | bit) and not member(eta & ~bit):
            total += weight(p, eta, n)
    return total


def is_increasing(member: Callable[[int], bool], n: int) -> bool:
    """Brute-force check that the event is monotone increasing."""
    for eta in all_masks(n):
        if not member(eta):
            continue
        for v in range(n):
            if not member(eta | (1 << v)):
                return False
    return True


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  A library of monotone events                                               #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def dictator(v: int) -> Callable[[int], bool]:
    """A = { eta : site v is open }.  The extremal (degree-one) event."""
    return lambda eta: bool((eta >> v) & 1)


def majority(n: int) -> Callable[[int], bool]:
    """A = { eta : strictly more than n/2 sites open }."""
    return lambda eta: 2 * popcount(eta) > n


def at_least(k: int) -> Callable[[int], bool]:
    """A = { eta : at least k sites open }."""
    return lambda eta: popcount(eta) >= k


def parity_free_or_and(n: int) -> Callable[[int], bool]:
    """Tribes-like event: OR over blocks of two of the AND inside each block."""
    blocks = [(2 * i, 2 * i + 1) for i in range(n // 2)]
    return lambda eta: any(((eta >> a) & 1) and ((eta >> b) & 1) for a, b in blocks)


def grid_crossing(m: int) -> Tuple[Callable[[int], bool], int]:
    """Left-to-right open crossing of the m x m grid (site percolation).

    Returns the membership predicate and the number of sites n = m*m.  Site
    (i, j) (row i, column j) is stored in bit i*m + j.
    """
    n = m * m

    def member(eta: int) -> bool:
        stack = [(i, 0) for i in range(m) if (eta >> (i * m)) & 1]
        seen = set(stack)
        while stack:
            i, j = stack.pop()
            if j == m - 1:
                return True
            for di, dj in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                a, b = i + di, j + dj
                if 0 <= a < m and 0 <= b < m and (a, b) not in seen:
                    if (eta >> (a * m + b)) & 1:
                        seen.add((a, b))
                        stack.append((a, b))
        return False

    return member, n


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Verification routines                                                      #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def check(label: str, lhs: Rat, rhs: Rat) -> bool:
    ok = lhs == rhs
    flag = "OK " if ok else "FAIL"
    print(f"  [{flag}] {label:<58} {str(lhs):>18} == {str(rhs):>18}")
    return ok


def demo_product_rule_and_orthogonality(n: int = 3, p: Rat = Rat(1, 3)) -> None:
    print(f"\n=== 1. Product rule and orthogonality  (n = {n}, p = {p}) ===")
    q = p * (1 - p)

    # Product rule for an arbitrary family of one-site functions.
    g = [(Rat(2, 5), Rat(-1, 7)), (Rat(3), Rat(1, 2)), (Rat(-4, 3), Rat(5, 6))]
    table = [Rat(1) for _ in all_masks(n)]
    for eta in all_masks(n):
        prod = Rat(1)
        for v in range(n):
            prod *= g[v][0] if (eta >> v) & 1 else g[v][1]
        table[eta] = prod
    lhs = expectation(p, table, n)
    rhs = Rat(1)
    for v in range(n):
        rhs *= p * g[v][0] + (1 - p) * g[v][1]
    check("E[prod_v g_v] = prod_v (p g_v(1) + (1-p) g_v(0))", lhs, rhs)

    # Full orthogonality of the characters.
    bad = 0
    for S in all_masks(n):
        for T in all_masks(n):
            val = sum(
                weight(p, eta, n) * psi_set(p, S, eta, n) * psi_set(p, T, eta, n)
                for eta in all_masks(n)
            )
            expect = q ** popcount(S) if S == T else Rat(0)
            if val != expect:
                bad += 1
    print(f"  [{'OK ' if bad == 0 else 'FAIL'}] "
          f"E[psi_S psi_T] = [S=T] q^|S| for all {4 ** n} pairs (S,T)")

    # Reproducing kernel.
    bad = 0
    for xi in all_masks(n):
        for eta in all_masks(n):
            ker = Rat(0)
            for S in all_masks(n):
                term = Rat(1)
                for v in range(n):
                    if (S >> v) & 1:
                        term *= psi(p, v, xi) * psi(p, v, eta) / q
                ker += term
            expect = 1 / weight(p, eta, n) if xi == eta else Rat(0)
            if ker != expect:
                bad += 1
    print(f"  [{'OK ' if bad == 0 else 'FAIL'}] "
          f"reproducing kernel = [xi=eta]/mu_p(eta) for all {4 ** n} pairs")


def demo_completeness_and_parseval(n: int = 4, p: Rat = Rat(2, 5)) -> None:
    print(f"\n=== 2. Completeness, Parseval, Efron-Stein defect "
          f"(arbitrary f; n = {n}, p = {p}) ===")
    q = p * (1 - p)

    # A deterministic but "generic" pair of rational functions on the cube.
    f = [Rat((7 * eta * eta + 3 * eta + 1) % 23 - 11, 5) for eta in all_masks(n)]
    g = [Rat((13 * eta + 5) % 17 - 8, 3) for eta in all_masks(n)]

    fh = fourier_coefficients(p, f, n)
    gh = fourier_coefficients(p, g, n)
    check("fast transform agrees with direct transform",
          sum(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(fh, fourier_coefficients_direct(p, f, n))),
          Rat(0))

    # Completeness: f = sum_S fhat(S) psi_S, pointwise.
    worst = Rat(0)
    for eta in all_masks(n):
        recon = sum(fh[S] * psi_set(p, S, eta, n) for S in all_masks(n))
        worst = max(worst, abs(recon - f[eta]))
    check("max_eta | f(eta) - sum_S fhat(S) psi_S(eta) |", worst, Rat(0))

    # Parseval.
    fg = [f[eta] * g[eta] for eta in all_masks(n)]
    check("E[f g] = sum_S q^|S| fhat(S) ghat(S)",
          expectation(p, fg, n),
          sum(q ** popcount(S) * fh[S] * gh[S] for S in all_masks(n)))

    # Variance form.
    ff = [x * x for x in f]
    var = expectation(p, ff, n) - expectation(p, f, n) ** 2
    energies = level_energies(p, fh, n)
    check("Var(f) = sum_{S != empty} w_S(f)",
          var, sum(energies[S] for S in all_masks(n) if S != 0))

    # Site energy identity and the exact Efron-Stein / Poincare defect.
    total_deriv = Rat(0)
    for v in range(n):
        dv = discrete_derivative(f, v, n)
        dv_sq = [x * x for x in dv]
        e_dv = expectation(p, dv_sq, n)
        total_deriv += e_dv
        site = sum(energies[S] for S in all_masks(n) if (S >> v) & 1)
        check(f"site energy above v={v}: sum_{{S ni v}} w_S = q E[(D_v f)^2]",
              site, q * e_dv)

    defect = sum(
        (Rat(popcount(S)) - 1) * energies[S] for S in all_masks(n) if S != 0
    )
    check("q sum_v E[(D_v f)^2] - Var(f) = sum_{S!=0}(|S|-1) w_S",
          q * total_deriv - var, defect)
    print(f"  defect = {defect}  (>= 0: {defect >= 0})")


def analyse_event(name: str, member: Callable[[int], bool], n: int, p: Rat,
                  verbose: bool = True) -> Dict[str, Rat]:
    """Full exact analysis of one increasing event at one density."""
    q = p * (1 - p)
    assert is_increasing(member, n), f"{name} is not increasing"

    P = event_probability(p, member, n)
    infl = [influence(p, member, v, n) for v in range(n)]
    g = sign_indicator(member, n)
    gh = fourier_coefficients(p, g, n)
    w = level_energies(p, gh, n)

    total_energy = sum(w)
    high = sum(w[S] for S in all_masks(n) if popcount(S) >= 2)
    poincare_defect = sum(
        (Rat(popcount(S)) - 1) * w[S] for S in all_masks(n) if S != 0
    )
    s1 = sum(infl)
    s2 = sum(x * x for x in infl)

    if verbose:
        print(f"\n--- {name}   (n = {n}, p = {p}) ---")
        print(f"  P = {P},   4P(1-P) = {4 * P * (1 - P)}")
        print(f"  influences        = {[str(x) for x in infl]}")
        print(f"  sum I_v  = {s1},   sum I_v^2 = {s2}")
        spectrum: Dict[int, Rat] = {}
        for S in all_masks(n):
            k = popcount(S)
            spectrum[k] = spectrum.get(k, Rat(0)) + w[S]
        print("  energy by level   = "
              + ", ".join(f"level {k}: {spectrum[k]}" for k in sorted(spectrum)
                          if spectrum[k] != 0))
        check("Plancherel: sum_S w_S = 1", total_energy, Rat(1))
        check("degree-0 coefficient = 2P - 1", gh[0], 2 * P - 1)
        for v in range(n):
            check(f"degree-1 coefficient at v={v} equals 2 I_v",
                  gh[1 << v], 2 * infl[v])
        check("energy decomposition: 4P(1-P) = 4q sum I_v^2 + high energy",
              4 * P * (1 - P), 4 * q * s2 + high)
        check("Poincare defect: 4q sum I_v - 4P(1-P) = sum (|S|-1) w_S",
              4 * q * s1 - 4 * P * (1 - P), poincare_defect)
        check("chaining: 4q( sum I_v - sum I_v^2 ) = sum_{|S|>=2} |S| w_S",
              4 * q * (s1 - s2),
              sum(Rat(popcount(S)) * w[S] for S in all_masks(n)
                  if popcount(S) >= 2))
        print(f"  l2 bound   q sum I_v^2 = {q * s2}  <=  P(1-P) = {P * (1 - P)}"
              f"   [slack {P * (1 - P) - q * s2}]")
        print(f"  Poincare   P(1-P) = {P * (1 - P)}  <=  q sum I_v = {q * s1}"
              f"   [slack {q * s1 - P * (1 - P)}]")
        print(f"  square-root law: (sum I_v)^2 = {s1 ** 2}  <=  "
              f"n P(1-P)/q = {n * P * (1 - P) / q}")
        tight = all(gh[S] == 0 for S in all_masks(n) if popcount(S) >= 2)
        print(f"  degree <= 1 (equality case of BOTH inequalities): {tight}")

    return {
        "P": P, "sum_I": s1, "sum_I2": s2,
        "high_energy": high, "poincare_defect": poincare_defect,
    }


def demo_monotone_events() -> None:
    print("\n=== 3. Monotone events: the two identities, exactly ===")
    analyse_event("Dictator on site 0, 3 sites", dictator(0), 3, Rat(1, 3))
    analyse_event("Majority of 3", majority(3), 3, Rat(1, 2))
    analyse_event("Majority of 3, biased", majority(3), 3, Rat(1, 4))
    analyse_event("AND of 3 sites (at least 3 open)", at_least(3), 3, Rat(2, 5))
    analyse_event("OR of 3 sites (at least 1 open)", at_least(1), 3, Rat(1, 5))
    analyse_event("Two blocks: (x0 AND x1) OR (x2 AND x3)",
                  parity_free_or_and(4), 4, Rat(1, 2))


def demo_grid_crossing() -> None:
    print("\n=== 4. Grid crossing (site percolation) ===")
    for m, p in ((2, Rat(1, 2)), (3, Rat(1, 2)), (3, Rat(3, 5))):
        member, n = grid_crossing(m)
        analyse_event(f"Left-right crossing of the {m}x{m} grid", member, n, p)


def demo_threshold_profile() -> None:
    """Watch the two defects as p sweeps across the threshold of a 3x3 crossing."""
    print("\n=== 5. Both defects across the threshold (3x3 crossing) ===")
    member, n = grid_crossing(3)
    print(f"  {'p':>6} {'P':>10} {'sum I_v':>10} {'l2 slack':>12} "
          f"{'Poincare slack':>16} {'high energy':>13}")
    for num in range(1, 10):
        p = Rat(num, 10)
        q = p * (1 - p)
        d = analyse_event("", member, n, p, verbose=False)
        l2_slack = d["P"] * (1 - d["P"]) - q * d["sum_I2"]
        po_slack = q * d["sum_I"] - d["P"] * (1 - d["P"])
        print(f"  {str(p):>6} {float(d['P']):>10.5f} {float(d['sum_I']):>10.5f} "
              f"{float(l2_slack):>12.6f} {float(po_slack):>16.6f} "
              f"{float(d['high_energy']):>13.6f}")
    print("  Both slacks vanish only for degree-<=1 events; a crossing is far")
    print("  from a dictator, so both stay strictly positive throughout.")


def demo_equality_case() -> None:
    """The unique tight events: constants and dictators."""
    print("\n=== 6. The shared equality case ===")
    n, p = 3, Rat(1, 3)
    q = p * (1 - p)
    for name, member in (("dictator on site 1", dictator(1)),
                         ("OR of 3 sites", at_least(1))):
        P = event_probability(p, member, n)
        infl = [influence(p, member, v, n) for v in range(n)]
        s1, s2 = sum(infl), sum(x * x for x in infl)
        print(f"  {name:<22}  q*sum I^2 = {q * s2},  P(1-P) = {P * (1 - P)},"
              f"  q*sum I = {q * s1}")
        print(f"  {'':<22}  l2 tight: {q * s2 == P * (1 - P)},"
              f"  Poincare tight: {P * (1 - P) == q * s1}")


def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 92)
    print("  p-BIASED FOURIER ANALYSIS ON THE DISCRETE CUBE  --  exact rational demo")
    print("=" * 92)
    demo_product_rule_and_orthogonality()
    demo_completeness_and_parseval()
    demo_monotone_events()
    demo_grid_crossing()
    demo_threshold_profile()
    demo_equality_case()
    print("\nAll identities above hold as exact equalities of rational numbers.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""
Exhaustive extremal search: over ALL monotone events on a small site set, verify
both influence inequalities and confirm that equality holds in each one exactly
for the events of Fourier degree at most one (the constants and the dictators),
and that the two equality cases coincide.

All arithmetic is exact (fractions.Fraction).

Inequalities checked, with q = p(1-p), P = mu_p(A), I_v the influence of site v:

    (L)  q * sum_v I_v^2  <=  P(1-P)          [ l^2 influence bound ]
    (P)  P(1-P)           <=  q * sum_v I_v   [ variance-influence / Poincare ]

and the exact identities that produce them,

    4P(1-P)          = 4q sum_v I_v^2 + sum_{|S|>=2} w_S
    4q sum_v I_v     = 4P(1-P) + sum_{S != empty} (|S|-1) w_S

where w_S = q^{|S|} * ghat(S)^2 is the biased Fourier energy of the +-1 indicator
of the event at the level S.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Rat = Fraction


def popcount(mask: int) -> int:
    return bin(mask).count("1")


def weight(p: Rat, eta: int, n: int) -> Rat:
    k = popcount(eta)
    return p ** k * (1 - p) ** (n - k)


def fourier_coefficients(p: Rat, table: Sequence[Rat], n: int) -> List[Rat]:
    """Biased fast Walsh transform: entry S becomes ghat(S).  Cost O(n 2^n)."""
    a = list(table)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for i in range(1 << n):
            if i & bit:
                continue
            hi, lo = a[i | bit], a[i]
            a[i] = p * hi + (1 - p) * lo
            a[i | bit] = hi - lo
    return a


def monotone_events(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All monotone increasing events on n sites, encoded as membership bitsets."""
    size = 1 << n
    out: List[int] = []
    for code in range(1 << size):
        ok = True
        for eta in range(size):
            if (code >> eta) & 1:
                for v in range(n):
                    if not ((code >> (eta | (1 << v))) & 1):
                        ok = False
                        break
            if not ok:
                break
        if ok:
            out.append(code)
    return out


def analyse(code: int, n: int, p: Rat) -> Dict[str, object]:
    size = 1 << n
    q = p * (1 - p)
    member = [bool((code >> eta) & 1) for eta in range(size)]
    g = [Rat(1) if member[eta] else Rat(-1) for eta in range(size)]
    P = sum(weight(p, eta, n) for eta in range(size) if member[eta])

    infl: List[Rat] = []
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        infl.append(sum(weight(p, eta, n) for eta in range(size)
                        if member[eta | bit] and not member[eta & ~bit]))

    gh = fourier_coefficients(p, g, n)
    w = [q ** popcount(S) * gh[S] ** 2 for S in range(size)]

    s1 = sum(infl)
    s2 = sum(x * x for x in infl)
    high = sum(w[S] for S in range(size) if popcount(S) >= 2)
    defect = sum((Rat(popcount(S)) - 1) * w[S] for S in range(size) if S != 0)
    degree = max((popcount(S) for S in range(size) if gh[S] != 0), default=0)

    assert sum(w) == 1, "Plancherel failed"
    assert 4 * P * (1 - P) == 4 * q * s2 + high, "energy decomposition failed"
    assert 4 * q * s1 - 4 * P * (1 - P) == defect, "Poincare defect failed"

    return {
        "P": P, "s1": s1, "s2": s2, "high": high, "defect": defect,
        "degree": degree,
        "l2_tight": q * s2 == P * (1 - P),
        "poincare_tight": P * (1 - P) == q * s1,
    }


def describe(code: int, n: int) -> str:
    size = 1 << n
    members = [eta for eta in range(size) if (code >> eta) & 1]
    if not members:
        return "empty event"
    if len(members) == size:
        return "full event"
    minimal = [eta for eta in members
               if not any((eta & ~(1 << v)) in members and (eta >> v) & 1
                          for v in range(n))]
    def show(eta: int) -> str:
        return "{" + ",".join(f"x{v}" for v in range(n) if (eta >> v) & 1) + "}"
    return "minimal open sets: " + " ".join(show(m) for m in minimal)


def main() -> None:
    n = 3
    p = Rat(1, 3)
    events = monotone_events(n)
    print(f"All monotone events on {n} sites at p = {p}: {len(events)} of them")
    print(f"{'degree':>7} {'P':>10} {'sum I':>10} {'sum I^2':>10} "
          f"{'l2 tight':>9} {'Poin tight':>11}  description")
    tight_both: List[int] = []
    for code in events:
        d = analyse(code, n, p)
        if d["l2_tight"] != d["poincare_tight"]:
            raise AssertionError("the two equality cases disagree!")
        if d["l2_tight"]:
            tight_both.append(code)
        print(f"{d['degree']:>7} {str(d['P']):>10} {str(d['s1']):>10} "
              f"{str(d['s2']):>10} {str(d['l2_tight']):>9} "
              f"{str(d['poincare_tight']):>11}  {describe(code, n)}")

    print()
    print(f"Events achieving equality in BOTH inequalities: {len(tight_both)}")
    for code in tight_both:
        d = analyse(code, n, p)
        print(f"  degree {d['degree']}: {describe(code, n)}")
    print("These are exactly the constants and the dictators, i.e. the events of")
    print("Fourier degree at most one -- as the two defect identities predict.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: The p-Biased Fast Walsh Transform and Its Exact Inverse
algorithms.description: Computes all 2^n biased Fourier coefficients of a function on the n-site cube in O(n 2^n) operations rather than the naive O(4^n n), and inverts the transform at the same cost. The mathematical foundation is the one-coordinate decomposition f = A_v f + psi_v D_v f, where A_v f is the average of f over the coordinate v and D_v f its discrete derivative: both are independent of v, and the Fourier coefficients of f at sets avoiding v are those of A_v f, while at sets containing v they are those of D_v f with v deleted. One pass over coordinate v therefore replaces each pair of table entries by that decomposition, and after n passes the slot indexed by the bitmask S holds exactly the coefficient at S. Because every operation is a rational combination of the inputs, running the transform on Fraction inputs gives exact coefficients; the inverse pass solves the same two-by-two system backwards and is, literally, the completeness theorem executed as an algorithm. Complexity: O(n 2^n) time, O(2^n) space.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT : density p, table F[0 .. 2^n - 1] of the function values,
        indexed by configuration bitmask (bit v set  <=>  site v open)
OUTPUT: table A[0 .. 2^n - 1] with A[S] = fhat(S), indexed by set bitmask

A <- copy of F
for v <- 0 to n-1 do
    bit <- 2^v
    for i <- 0 to 2^n - 1 do
        if (i AND bit) != 0 then continue          // visit each pair once
        hi <- A[i OR bit]                          // value with site v open
        lo <- A[i]                                 // value with site v closed
        A[i]       <- p*hi + (1-p)*lo              // (A_v f):  slot without v
        A[i OR bit] <- hi - lo                     // (D_v f):  slot with v
    end for
end for
return A

INVERSE (undo the butterfly, coordinates in reverse order)
for v <- n-1 downto 0 do
    bit <- 2^v
    for i <- 0 to 2^n - 1 do
        if (i AND bit) != 0 then continue
        x <- A[i]; y <- A[i OR bit]
        A[i OR bit] <- x + (1-p)*y                 // value with v open
        A[i]        <- x - p*y                     // value with v closed
    end for
end for
return A
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: the p-biased fast Walsh transform.

Computes, for a real function f on the cube {0,1}^n given as a table of 2^n
values, all 2^n biased Fourier coefficients

        fhat(S) = E_p[ f * psi_S ] / (p(1-p))^{|S|},
        psi_v(eta) = 1-p if eta_v = 1 else -p,     psi_S = prod_{v in S} psi_v,

in O(n 2^n) operations and O(1) extra memory.  With Fraction inputs the output
is exact.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, TypeVar

Num = TypeVar("Num", float, Fraction)


def biased_walsh_transform(p: Num, table: Sequence[Num], n: int) -> List[Num]:
    """In-place-style butterfly transform; entry S of the result is fhat(S).

    Correctness.  One pass over coordinate v replaces the pair of table entries
    (f(eta^{v->1}), f(eta^{v->0})) by ((A_v f)(eta), (D_v f)(eta)) where

        A_v f = p f(.^{v->1}) + (1-p) f(.^{v->0}),   D_v f = f(.^{v->1}) - f(.^{v->0}),

    which is exactly the one-coordinate decomposition f = A_v f + psi_v D_v f.
    For a set S avoiding v one has fhat(S) = (A_v f)^(S), and for S containing v
    one has fhat(S) = (D_v f)^(S \\ {v}); so after processing every coordinate the
    slot whose bitmask is S carries fhat(S).
    """
    a: List[Num] = list(table)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for i in range(1 << n):
            if i & bit:
                continue
            hi, lo = a[i | bit], a[i]
            a[i] = p * hi + (1 - p) * lo        # A_v f  -> slot without v
            a[i | bit] = hi - lo                # D_v f  -> slot with v
    return a


def inverse_biased_walsh_transform(p: Num, coeffs: Sequence[Num],
                                   n: int) -> List[Num]:
    """The inverse transform: reconstruct f from its coefficients.

    Undoing the butterfly means solving  a = p*hi + (1-p)*lo,  b = hi - lo  for
    (hi, lo), i.e.  hi = a + (1-p) b,  lo = a - p b.  This is the completeness
    theorem f = sum_S fhat(S) psi_S in algorithmic form, and costs O(n 2^n).
    """
    a: List[Num] = list(coeffs)
    for v in reversed(range(n)):
        bit = 1 << v
        for i in range(1 << n):
            if i & bit:
                continue
            x, y = a[i], a[i | bit]
            a[i | bit] = x + (1 - p) * y
            a[i] = x - p * y
    return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 4
    p = Fraction(2, 5)
    f = [Fraction((7 * e * e + 3 * e + 1) % 23 - 11, 5) for e in range(1 << n)]
    fh = biased_walsh_transform(p, f, n)
    back = inverse_biased_walsh_transform(p, fh, n)
    print("exact round trip:", back == f)
    print("fhat(empty) = E[f] =", fh[0])

algorithms.name: Exact Influence-and-Defect Ledger of a Monotone Event
algorithms.description: Given an increasing event on n sites specified by a membership predicate, and a rational density p, this routine computes in O(n 2^n) exact rational operations the event probability, the influence of every site, the full Fourier energy spectrum of the plus-or-minus-one indicator, the l-squared remainder (the energy carried by levels of size at least two) and the Poincare defect (the energy weighted by level size minus one). It first certifies monotonicity by checking membership is preserved under opening any single site, then asserts the three exact identities that constitute the main theory: total energy equals one (the biased Plancherel identity), the energy decomposition, and the Poincare defect identity. Because the assertions are exact rational equalities, any error in the theory or the implementation would raise immediately. The returned degree of the event decides, by the equality theorems, whether both inequalities are simultaneously tight.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT : density p (rational), membership predicate member(.), number of sites n
OUTPUT: P, influences I[0..n-1], level energies w[.], l^2 remainder, Poincare defect

q <- p*(1-p)
for each configuration e do
    W[e]   <- p^popcount(e) * (1-p)^(n - popcount(e))
    inA[e] <- member(e)

// certify monotonicity
for each e with inA[e] do
    for v <- 0 to n-1 do
        if not inA[e OR 2^v] then FAIL 'event is not increasing'

P <- sum of W[e] over e with inA[e]
for v <- 0 to n-1 do
    I[v] <- sum of W[e] over all e with  inA[e OR 2^v] and not inA[e AND NOT 2^v]

G[e] <- +1 if inA[e] else -1                      // the sign indicator
GH   <- BiasedFastWalshTransform(p, G, n)         // Algorithm 1
for each set S do  w[S] <- q^|S| * GH[S]^2

s1 <- sum_v I[v] ;  s2 <- sum_v I[v]^2
high   <- sum of w[S] over |S| >= 2
defect <- sum of (|S| - 1) * w[S] over S nonempty
degree <- max |S| with GH[S] != 0

ASSERT  sum_S w[S] = 1                            // Plancherel
ASSERT  4*P*(1-P)      = 4*q*s2 + high             // energy decomposition
ASSERT  4*q*s1 - 4*P*(1-P) = defect                // Poincare defect
return (P, I, w, high, defect, degree)
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: the exact influence-and-defect ledger of a monotone event.

Given a monotone (increasing) event A on n sites and a density p, computes in
O(n 2^n) exact rational operations:

    P            = mu_p(A),
    I_v          = mu_p(Piv_v(A))                 the influence of each site,
    w_S          = (p(1-p))^{|S|} ghat(S)^2       the Fourier energy of the
                                                  +-1 indicator g at each level,
    high         = sum_{|S| >= 2} w_S             the l^2 remainder,
    defect       = sum_{S != empty} (|S|-1) w_S   the Poincare defect,

and certifies the two exact identities

    4P(1-P)          = 4 p(1-p) sum_v I_v^2  +  high,
    4 p(1-p) sum_v I_v = 4P(1-P)             +  defect,

from which the l^2 influence bound and the variance-influence (Poincare)
inequality follow, both with equality precisely when the event has Fourier
degree at most one.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Dict, List

Rat = Fraction


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    return bin(x).count("1")


def ledger(p: Rat, member: Callable[[int], bool], n: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    size = 1 << n
    q = p * (1 - p)

    # measure and membership tables
    weight = [p ** popcount(e) * (1 - p) ** (n - popcount(e)) for e in range(size)]
    inA = [member(e) for e in range(size)]

    # monotonicity check (O(n 2^n))
    for e in range(size):
        if inA[e]:
            for v in range(n):
                if not inA[e | (1 << v)]:
                    raise ValueError("event is not increasing")

    P = sum(weight[e] for e in range(size) if inA[e])

    influences: List[Rat] = []
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        influences.append(sum(weight[e] for e in range(size)
                              if inA[e | bit] and not inA[e & ~bit]))

    # +-1 indicator and its spectrum by the biased fast Walsh transform
    a: List[Rat] = [Rat(1) if inA[e] else Rat(-1) for e in range(size)]
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for i in range(size):
            if i & bit:
                continue
            hi, lo = a[i | bit], a[i]
            a[i] = p * hi + (1 - p) * lo
            a[i | bit] = hi - lo
    energy = [q ** popcount(S) * a[S] ** 2 for S in range(size)]

    s1 = sum(influences)
    s2 = sum(x * x for x in influences)
    high = sum(energy[S] for S in range(size) if popcount(S) >= 2)
    defect = sum((Rat(popcount(S)) - 1) * energy[S] for S in range(size) if S)
    degree = max((popcount(S) for S in range(size) if a[S] != 0), default=0)

    assert sum(energy) == 1
    assert 4 * P * (1 - P) == 4 * q * s2 + high
    assert 4 * q * s1 - 4 * P * (1 - P) == defect

    return {
        "P": P, "influences": influences, "sum_I": s1, "sum_I2": s2,
        "energy": energy, "l2_remainder": high, "poincare_defect": defect,
        "degree": degree,
        "l2_tight": high == 0, "poincare_tight": defect == 0,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n, p = 3, Rat(1, 2)
    for name, ev in (("majority of 3", lambda e: popcount(e) >= 2),
                     ("dictator", lambda e: bool(e & 1)),
                     ("OR of 3", lambda e: e != 0)):
        d = ledger(p, ev, n)
        print(f"{name:<14} P={d['P']}  sum I={d['sum_I']}  degree={d['degree']}  "
              f"l2 remainder={d['l2_remainder']}  Poincare defect={d['poincare_defect']}"
              f"  both tight={d['l2_tight'] and d['poincare_tight']}")

algorithms.name: Reproducing-Kernel Reconstruction: a Completeness Certificate
algorithms.description: Builds the full kernel matrix K(xi, eta) = sum over all site sets S of the product over v in S of psi_v(xi) psi_v(eta) divided by p(1-p), in O(n 4^n) exact rational operations, and verifies that it equals the reciprocal of the measure on the diagonal and zero off it. This is the single computation on which completeness of the biased character system rests: a sum over subsets of a product is a product of binomials, and a single coordinate at which the two configurations disagree contributes the factor zero, annihilating the whole product. The routine then reconstructs an arbitrary function from the kernel, certifying that expanding in the characters loses no information. For production use the O(n 2^n) inverse transform of Algorithm 1 is preferable; this routine exists to exhibit the mechanism and to provide an independent check of it.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT : density p (rational, strictly between 0 and 1), number of sites n
OUTPUT: TRUE if the character system is complete on this site set

q <- p*(1-p)
for each pair of configurations (xi, eta) do
    K[xi][eta] <- 1
    for v <- 0 to n-1 do
        psi_xi  <- (1-p) if xi_v  = open else -p
        psi_eta <- (1-p) if eta_v = open else -p
        K[xi][eta] <- K[xi][eta] * ( 1 + psi_xi*psi_eta/q )

for each pair (xi, eta) do
    expected <- 1/mu_p(eta)   if xi = eta   else 0
    if K[xi][eta] != expected then return FALSE
return TRUE

RECONSTRUCTION (the completeness theorem in kernel form)
for each configuration eta do
    F[eta] <- sum over xi of  mu_p(xi) * f(xi) * K[xi][eta]
// F equals f exactly
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: reproducing-kernel reconstruction (a completeness certificate).

The biased characters psi_S, S ranging over all subsets of the n sites, satisfy
the reproducing-kernel identity

    K_p(xi, eta) := sum_S prod_{v in S} [ psi_v(xi) psi_v(eta) / (p(1-p)) ]
                  = 1/mu_p(eta)   if xi = eta,     0 otherwise,

because the sum over subsets is the product prod_v ( 1 + psi_v(xi)psi_v(eta)/q )
and a single disagreeing coordinate contributes the factor 0.

This routine builds the full 2^n x 2^n kernel matrix in O(n 4^n) exact rational
operations and uses it to reconstruct an arbitrary function from its Fourier
coefficients, thereby certifying completeness of the character system on the
given site set.  (For production use the O(n 2^n) inverse transform instead;
this routine exists to exhibit the mechanism.)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence

Rat = Fraction


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    return bin(x).count("1")


def psi(p: Rat, v: int, eta: int) -> Rat:
    """The centred one-site character."""
    return (1 - p) if (eta >> v) & 1 else -p


def weight(p: Rat, eta: int, n: int) -> Rat:
    k = popcount(eta)
    return p ** k * (1 - p) ** (n - k)


def kernel_matrix(p: Rat, n: int) -> List[List[Rat]]:
    """K[xi][eta] = prod_v ( 1 + psi_v(xi) psi_v(eta) / (p(1-p)) )."""
    q = p * (1 - p)
    size = 1 << n
    K: List[List[Rat]] = []
    for xi in range(size):
        row: List[Rat] = []
        for eta in range(size):
            prod = Rat(1)
            for v in range(n):
                prod *= 1 + psi(p, v, xi) * psi(p, v, eta) / q
            row.append(prod)
        K.append(row)
    return K


def certify_completeness(p: Rat, n: int) -> bool:
    """Check that the kernel is the measure-weighted delta function."""
    K = kernel_matrix(p, n)
    for xi in range(1 << n):
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            expected = 1 / weight(p, eta, n) if xi == eta else Rat(0)
            if K[xi][eta] != expected:
                return False
    return True


def reconstruct(p: Rat, table: Sequence[Rat], n: int) -> List[Rat]:
    """f(eta) = sum_xi mu_p(xi) f(xi) K(xi, eta), by the kernel identity."""
    K = kernel_matrix(p, n)
    out: List[Rat] = []
    for eta in range(1 << n):
        out.append(sum(weight(p, xi, n) * table[xi] * K[xi][eta]
                       for xi in range(1 << n)))
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n, p = 3, Rat(1, 3)
    print("kernel is a weighted delta:", certify_completeness(p, n))
    f = [Rat((5 * e + 2) % 11 - 5, 4) for e in range(1 << n)]
    print("reconstruction is exact:", reconstruct(p, f, n) == f)

visualizations.name: Fourier Energy Profiles of Monotone Events: Where the Mass Lives
visualizations.description: Four bar charts showing, at density one half, the biased Fourier energy of a dictator, of majority on three sites, of an AND-OR event on four sites, and of the left-right crossing of the three-by-three grid, grouped by level. Every profile has total mass exactly one -- the Plancherel identity -- and the levels zero and one are drawn in grey because both influence inequalities charge nothing for them, while the levels of size at least two are drawn in indigo because they are precisely what both inequalities pay for. The panel titles report the two resulting defects: the l-squared remainder (the indigo mass) and the Poincare defect (the indigo mass weighted by level size minus one). The dictator's profile lives entirely in the grey region and both its defects are zero; the crossing spreads its mass far up the ladder.
visualizations.code:
"""
Visualization: the Fourier energy spectrum, by level, of several monotone events
on the biased cube -- and the two influence inequalities read off that spectrum.

For a monotone event A with +-1 indicator g, the biased Fourier energies
w_S = (p(1-p))^{|S|} ghat(S)^2 are nonnegative and sum to 1.  Grouping them by
level k = |S| gives a probability distribution on {0, 1, ..., n}, the "energy
profile" of the event.  Both classical influence inequalities are integrals of
this profile against a weight vanishing on levels 0 and 1:

    l^2 influence bound   <->   weight  1{k >= 2}
    Poincare inequality   <->   weight  k - 1

The figure shows the profiles of a dictator (all mass on levels 0 and 1: both
inequalities are tight), majority of 3, an AND-OR event, and the left-right
crossing of the 3x3 grid, together with the two weighted integrals.

Run:  python viz_spectrum.py     (writes energy_spectrum.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def popcount(mask: int) -> int:
    return bin(mask).count("1")


def biased_transform(p: float, table: List[float], n: int) -> List[float]:
    """Biased fast Walsh transform; entry S becomes ghat(S).  O(n 2^n)."""
    a = list(table)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for i in range(1 << n):
            if i & bit:
                continue
            hi, lo = a[i | bit], a[i]
            a[i] = p * hi + (1.0 - p) * lo
            a[i | bit] = hi - lo
    return a


def energy_profile(p: float, member: Callable[[int], bool], n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    q = p * (1.0 - p)
    g = [1.0 if member(eta) else -1.0 for eta in range(1 << n)]
    gh = biased_transform(p, g, n)
    prof = np.zeros(n + 1)
    for S in range(1 << n):
        k = popcount(S)
        prof[k] += (q ** k) * gh[S] ** 2
    return prof


def grid_crossing(m: int) -> Tuple[Callable[[int], bool], int]:
    n = m * m

    def member(eta: int) -> bool:
        stack = [(i, 0) for i in range(m) if (eta >> (i * m)) & 1]
        seen = set(stack)
        while stack:
            i, j = stack.pop()
            if j == m - 1:
                return True
            for di, dj in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                a, b = i + di, j + dj
                if 0 <= a < m and 0 <= b < m and (a, b) not in seen \
                        and (eta >> (a * m + b)) & 1:
                    seen.add((a, b))
                    stack.append((a, b))
        return False

    return member, n


def main() -> None:
    p = 0.5
    cross, n_cross = grid_crossing(3)
    events: List[Tuple[str, Callable[[int], bool], int]] = [
        ("Dictator (1 of 3 sites)", lambda e: bool(e & 1), 3),
        ("Majority of 3", lambda e: popcount(e) >= 2, 3),
        ("(x0 AND x1) OR (x2 AND x3)",
         lambda e: bool((e & 3) == 3 or (e & 12) == 12), 4),
        ("Crossing of the 3x3 grid", cross, n_cross),
    ]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
    for ax, (name, member, n) in zip(axes.flat, events):
        prof = energy_profile(p, member, n)
        levels = np.arange(n + 1)
        colors = ["#94a3b8" if k <= 1 else "#6366f1" for k in levels]
        ax.bar(levels, prof, color=colors, edgecolor="#1e293b", linewidth=0.6)
        l2_gap = prof[2:].sum()                       # weight 1{k>=2}
        po_gap = float(((levels - 1) * prof)[1:].sum())  # weight k-1
        ax.set_title(f"{name}\n"
                     f"$\\ell^2$ remainder $= {l2_gap:.4f}$,   "
                     f"Poincaré defect $= {po_gap:.4f}$", fontsize=10)
        ax.set_xlabel("level $k=|S|$")
        ax.set_ylabel("energy $\\sum_{|S|=k} w_S$")
        ax.set_xticks(levels)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
        ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)
    fig.suptitle("Biased Fourier energy profiles at $p=1/2$: total mass is always $1$;\n"
                 "grey levels $0,1$ are free, indigo levels $\\geq 2$ pay for both "
                 "inequalities", fontsize=12)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.94))
    fig.savefig("energy_spectrum.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote energy_spectrum.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""
Visualization: the influence sandwich across the density.

For an increasing event A on n sites, with q = p(1-p), P = mu_p(A) and influences
I_v, the two exact identities

    4P(1-P)      = 4q sum_v I_v^2 + sum_{|S|>=2} w_S,
    4q sum_v I_v = 4P(1-P) + sum_{S != empty} (|S|-1) w_S

sandwich the variance:

    q sum_v I_v^2   <=   P(1-P)   <=   q sum_v I_v .

This script plots all three curves for the left-right crossing of the 3x3 grid as
p sweeps from 0 to 1, shading the two gaps -- each of which is an explicitly
computable Fourier energy, and each of which closes only for events of degree at
most one.  The right-hand panel plots the two gaps themselves, showing that they
peak together near the threshold, where the event is most "collective".

Run:  python viz_sandwich.py     (writes influence_sandwich.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def popcount(mask: int) -> int:
    return bin(mask).count("1")


def grid_crossing(m: int) -> Tuple[Callable[[int], bool], int]:
    n = m * m

    def member(eta: int) -> bool:
        stack = [(i, 0) for i in range(m) if (eta >> (i * m)) & 1]
        seen = set(stack)
        while stack:
            i, j = stack.pop()
            if j == m - 1:
                return True
            for di, dj in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                a, b = i + di, j + dj
                if 0 <= a < m and 0 <= b < m and (a, b) not in seen \
                        and (eta >> (a * m + b)) & 1:
                    seen.add((a, b))
                    stack.append((a, b))
        return False

    return member, n


def stats(p: float, member: Callable[[int], bool], n: int
          ) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Return (P, sum_v I_v, sum_v I_v^2) at density p."""
    size = 1 << n
    pc = np.array([popcount(e) for e in range(size)])
    w = (p ** pc) * ((1.0 - p) ** (n - pc))
    inA = np.array([1.0 if member(e) else 0.0 for e in range(size)])
    P = float(w @ inA)
    infl: List[float] = []
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        piv = np.array([
            1.0 if (member(e | bit) and not member(e & ~bit)) else 0.0
            for e in range(size)
        ])
        infl.append(float(w @ piv))
    arr = np.array(infl)
    return P, float(arr.sum()), float((arr ** 2).sum())


def main() -> None:
    member, n = grid_crossing(3)
    ps = np.linspace(0.02, 0.98, 97)
    var, lo, hi = [], [], []
    for p in ps:
        P, s1, s2 = stats(float(p), member, n)
        q = p * (1 - p)
        var.append(P * (1 - P))
        lo.append(q * s2)
        hi.append(q * s1)
    var, lo, hi = np.array(var), np.array(lo), np.array(hi)

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    ax1.fill_between(ps, lo, var, color="#a5b4fc", alpha=0.55,
                     label=r"$\ell^2$ remainder $=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{|S|\geq 2}w_S$")
    ax1.fill_between(ps, var, hi, color="#fca5a5", alpha=0.55,
                     label=r"Poincaré defect $=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{S}(|S|-1)w_S$")
    ax1.plot(ps, lo, color="#4338ca", lw=2, label=r"$p(1-p)\sum_v I_v^2$")
    ax1.plot(ps, var, color="#111827", lw=2.5, label=r"$P(1-P)$")
    ax1.plot(ps, hi, color="#b91c1c", lw=2, label=r"$p(1-p)\sum_v I_v$")
    ax1.set_xlabel("density $p$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("value")
    ax1.set_title("The influence sandwich for the $3\\times3$ grid crossing")
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.25)

    ax2.plot(ps, var - lo, color="#4338ca", lw=2, label=r"$\ell^2$ remainder")
    ax2.plot(ps, hi - var, color="#b91c1c", lw=2, label="Poincaré defect")
    ax2.set_xlabel("density $p$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("gap")
    ax2.set_title("Both gaps are high-level Fourier energy;\n"
                  "they peak together where the event is most collective")
    ax2.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("influence_sandwich.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote influence_sandwich.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.description: A single self-contained widget in which the reader chooses the number of sites, the monotone event (dictator, threshold, tribes, a square-grid crossing, or a freshly rolled random monotone event) and the density, and immediately sees three linked views of the same underlying object. First, the Fourier energy spectrum grouped by level, drawn live on a canvas, with levels zero and one greyed out because both inequalities let them pass free and the higher levels highlighted because both inequalities charge for them; the displayed total is always one, which is the Plancherel identity in action. Second, a sandwich bar whose full width is the per-site variance times the total influence, whose black tick marks the variance of the event, and whose two coloured segments are exactly the l-squared remainder and the Poincare defect -- so the reader watches the two classical inequalities squeeze the variance from opposite sides. Third, a per-site table checking, numerically and site by site, that the Fourier energy stored above a site equals four times the per-site variance times that site's influence. Three running equation lines report both defect identities and the chaining identity with their numerical values on each side. Selecting the dictator collapses both gaps to zero and flips the tightness badge to green, exhibiting live the theorem that the two inequalities share their equality case -- the events of Fourier degree at most one.

The Influence Ledger

Every monotone event on a finite set of sites has a Fourier energy spectrum: a nonnegative number wS for each set of sites S, always summing to 1. Two classical inequalities that bracket the event's variance from opposite sides — the ℓ2 influence bound and the variance–influence (Poincaré) inequality — are nothing but this one spectrum read against two different weights. Move the density slider, change the event, and watch both ledgers balance to the last digit.

Controls

Summary

P = μp(A)—
variance P(1−P)—
Σv Iv—
Σv Iv²—
Fourier degree—
total energy ΣS wS—
The total energy is exactly 1 for every ±1-valued function: that is the Plancherel identity, and it is the conservation law both inequalities spend.

Energy spectrum by level

levels 0–1 (free) levels ≥ 2 (paid for by both inequalities)

The sandwich

p(1−p)ΣIv² ℓ2 remainder Poincaré defect   (black tick = P(1−P), full width = p(1−p)ΣIv)
Both inequalities tight? no — equality holds in both exactly when the event has no energy above level 1, i.e. for constants and dictators.

Per-site influences and the site energy identity

The energy stored above a site, ΣS ∋ v wS, equals 4p(1−p) Iv — the biased form of the identity relating a coordinate's influence to the Fourier weight it carries. Summing over sites counts each level S exactly |S| times, which is where the factor |S|−1 in the Poincaré defect comes from.

# The Accounting of Influence ### A guided tour of biased Fourier analysis on the discrete cube, and of the one identity behind two opposite laws --- ## 1. The question Picture a large square grid of tiny valves. Each valve is independently **open** with probability $p$ and **closed** with probability $1-p$. Water is poured in at the left edge. Does it reach the right? This is the model question of *percolation*, and it stands in for a whole family of others: is a random network connected? is a random formula satisfiable? does a noisy election flip? All of them share two features. They are **monotone** — opening one more valve never hurts — and they exhibit a **sharp threshold**: below a critical density the answer is essentially always "no", above it essentially always "yes", and the transition happens in a window that narrows as the system grows. The classical explanation runs through *influence*. Our goal on this page is to show that the two central theorems about influence — which point in **opposite** directions and are usually proved by unrelated arguments — are in fact the same statement, read twice. --- ## 2. The vocabulary, in one screen Let $V$ be a finite set of **sites**, $n = |V|$. A **configuration** $\eta$ says, for each site, open or closed. Under the $p$-biased product measure, $$\mu_p(\eta) = p^{\,\#\text{open}}\,(1-p)^{\,\#\text{closed}}.$$ An event $A$ is **increasing** if opening more sites never removes you from $A$. Write $P = \mu_p(A)$. A site $v$ is **pivotal** at $\eta$ if the outcome hangs on it alone: opening $v$ puts you in $A$, closing $v$ puts you out. Its **influence** is $$I_v = \mu_p\big(\{\eta : v \text{ is pivotal}\}\big),$$ the probability that $v$ is the swing voter.
Two classical theorems that bracket the influences (click to expand) Write $q = p(1-p)$ for the per-site variance. Then, for every increasing event: **Variance–influence (Poincaré) inequality.** $$P(1-P) \;\le\; q\sum_v I_v.$$ Together with [Russo's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo%27s_formula) $\frac{dP}{dp} = \sum_v I_v$, this is the differential inequality $P(1-P) \le q\,P'$, and integrating it is what *proves* thresholds are sharp. **The $\ell^2$ influence bound.** $$q\sum_v I_v^2 \;\le\; P(1-P).$$ With Cauchy–Schwarz this gives the **square-root law** $\big(\sum_v I_v\big)^2 \le n\,P(1-P)/q$ — at $p=1/2$, no monotone event on $n$ sites has total influence above $\sqrt n$, so no threshold window is narrower than order $n^{-1/2}$. Majority attains it. One says the influences are *big enough*; the other says they are *not too big*.
--- ## 3. Frequencies for coin flips At $p = 1/2$ there is a classical Fourier theory of Boolean functions: encode open/closed as $\pm1$ and expand in the multilinear monomials $\prod_{v\in S}x_v$. See [*Analysis of Boolean Functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10386) for the full story. Percolation does not live at $p = 1/2$, and the $\pm1$ encoding stops being orthogonal the moment the coin is biased. The right replacement is a **centred character** per site, $$\psi_v(\eta) = \begin{cases}1-p & v\text{ open},\\ -p & v\text{ closed},\end{cases} \qquad \psi_S = \prod_{v\in S}\psi_v,\quad \psi_\emptyset = 1,$$ which has mean $0$ and variance $q = p(1-p)$. Everything below flows from one nearly self-evident statement. > **The Product Rule.** For any one-site functions $g_v$, > $$\mathbb{E}_p\Big[\prod_v g_v(\eta_v)\Big] = \prod_v\Big(p\,g_v(\text{open}) + (1-p)\,g_v(\text{closed})\Big).$$ This *is* independence of the sites. Orthogonality follows in a line: > **Orthogonality.** $\mathbb{E}_p[\psi_S\psi_T] = 0$ unless $S = T$, in which case it is $q^{|S|}$.
Why: the one-coordinate arithmetic (click to reveal) Apply the product rule to $\psi_S\psi_T$, which is a product of one-site functions. Coordinate $v$ contributes * $1$ if $v \notin S\cup T$; * $p(1-p) + (1-p)(-p) = 0$ if $v$ lies in exactly one of $S,T$ — this single zero kills the whole product; * $p(1-p)^2 + (1-p)p^2 = p(1-p) = q$ if $v \in S\cap T$. So the expectation is $q^{|S|}$ when $S=T$ and $0$ otherwise. $\blacksquare$
Define the **Fourier coefficient** and the **energy at level $S$**: $$\hat f(S) = \frac{\mathbb{E}_p[f\,\psi_S]}{q^{|S|}},\qquad w_S = q^{|S|}\hat f(S)^2 \ \ge 0.$$ Note $\hat f(\emptyset) = \mathbb{E}_p[f]$. --- ## 4. Computing the spectrum: one butterfly per coordinate Before any theory, let's be able to *compute*. The transform factorises coordinate by coordinate, and the resulting algorithm is a biased cousin of the fast Walsh–Hadamard transform: $O(n2^n)$ operations, exact in rational arithmetic. {{algorithm:0}} The inverse transform in that code is, quite literally, the completeness theorem executed in reverse. --- ## 5. Why the basis misses nothing Orthogonality alone gives only *Bessel's inequality*. To upgrade inequalities to identities we need **completeness**, and completeness follows from one delightful computation. > **The Reproducing Kernel Identity.** For $0 $$K(\xi,\eta) := \sum_{S\subseteq V}\prod_{v\in S}\frac{\psi_v(\xi)\psi_v(\eta)}{q} > = \begin{cases}1/\mu_p(\eta) & \xi = \eta,\\ 0 & \xi \ne \eta.\end{cases}$$
The whole proof (click to reveal) A sum over all subsets of a product is a product of binomials: $$K(\xi,\eta) = \prod_{v}\Big(1 + \frac{\psi_v(\xi)\psi_v(\eta)}{q}\Big).$$ Look at one factor. If $\xi,\eta$ **disagree** at $v$, the numerator is $(1-p)(-p) = -q$ and the factor is exactly $0$ — one disagreement annihilates everything. If both are open, the factor is $1 + \frac{(1-p)^2}{p(1-p)} = \frac1p$; if both closed, $1 + \frac{p^2}{p(1-p)} = \frac1{1-p}$. Multiplying the diagonal factors gives $1/\mu_p(\eta)$. $\blacksquare$
Two corollaries are immediate: > **Completeness.** $f = \sum_S \hat f(S)\,\psi_S$ for every $f$ and every $0 > **Parseval.** $\mathbb{E}_p[fg] = \sum_S q^{|S|}\hat f(S)\hat g(S)$; in particular $\operatorname{Var}_p(f) = \sum_{S\ne\emptyset}w_S$. The variance is the total energy off the empty set — and **every term is nonnegative**. That is the conservation law we are about to spend twice. {{algorithm:2}} --- ## 6. The ledger, made visible Now let $A$ be increasing and $g = \mathbf 1_A - \mathbf 1_{A^c}$ its $\pm1$ indicator. Three facts pin it down: - $\hat g(\emptyset) = 2P-1$; - $\hat g(\{v\}) = 2I_v$ — **the degree-one spectrum *is* the influence vector**; - $g^2 \equiv 1$, so by Parseval $\sum_S w_S = 1$: **all the energy of a Boolean function sums to one**. Split that total mass by level. Since $1 - (2P-1)^2 = 4P(1-P)$: > **Energy Decomposition.** $\displaystyle 4P(1-P) = 4q\sum_v I_v^2 + \underbrace{\sum_{|S|\ge2}w_S}_{\ \ge\,0}.$ The $\ell^2$ influence bound is *exactly* the statement that the last term is nonnegative. And because we know it exactly, we know when the bound is tight. The other inequality is the same ledger with a different weight. Writing $D_vf(\eta) = f(\eta^{v\to\text{open}}) - f(\eta^{v\to\text{closed}})$: > **Site Energy Identity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{S\ni v}w_S(f) = q\,\mathbb{E}_p\big[(D_vf)^2\big]$ for *every* real function $f$. Summing over $v$ counts each level $S$ exactly $|S|$ times; subtracting Parseval's variance $\sum_{S\ne\emptyset}w_S$ leaves: > **Exact Efron–Stein / Poincaré Defect.** For every $f$, > $$q\sum_v\mathbb{E}_p[(D_vf)^2] - \operatorname{Var}_p(f) = \sum_{S\ne\emptyset}\big(|S|-1\big)w_S \ \ge\ 0 .$$ > For an increasing event, $\mathbb{E}_p[(D_vg)^2] = 4I_v$, so this reads > $$4q\sum_v I_v - 4P(1-P) = \sum_{S\ne\emptyset}\big(|S|-1\big)w_S .$$ Two weights on the same nonnegative spectrum: | Inequality | Weight on $w_S$ | Vanishes when | |---|---|---| | $\ell^2$ influence bound | $\mathbf 1\{|S|\ge2\}$ | no energy above level 1 | | Poincaré / variance–influence | $|S|-1$ | no energy above level 1 | Same equality case. That is the punchline, and the widget below lets you feel it. --- ## 7. Play with the ledger Move the density slider and change the event. Watch three things at once: the energy profile (which always totals $1$), the sandwich bar (whose two coloured gaps are the two defects), and the per-site check that the energy above a site equals $4p(1-p)I_v$. Pick the **dictator** and both gaps collapse to zero — the unique tight case. Pick a grid crossing and both gaps swell where the event is most collective. {{interactive_demo:0}} --- ## 8. Reading the spectra Different events store their energy at very different levels. A dictator puts everything at levels $0$ and $1$. Majority of three puts $3/4$ at level one and $1/4$ at level three. A grid crossing spreads its energy far up the ladder — which is precisely why no single valve decides a crossing, and why both defects are large. {{visualization:0}} Sweeping the density traces the whole sandwich at once. Both gaps are high-level energy; they rise and fall together, peaking near the threshold. {{visualization:1}} --- ## 9. Check it yourself, exactly Everything above is finite algebra, so it can be verified as **exact rational arithmetic** — no floating point, no tolerance. The suite below reproduces the product rule, orthogonality, the reproducing kernel, completeness, Parseval, Plancherel, the energy decomposition, the site energy identity and the Efron–Stein defect, on random functions and on a library of monotone events including grid crossings. {{demo:0}} {{algorithm:1}} And here is the sharpest possible test of the equality case: enumerate **every** monotone event on three sites (there are $20$), and check that the two inequalities are tight for exactly the same five events — the two constants and the three dictators. {{demo:1}} --- ## 10. Where this goes next The two weights we used, $\mathbf 1\{|S|\ge2\}$ and $|S|-1$, are the simplest members of a family: any nonnegative weight vanishing on levels $0$ and $1$ gives an inequality. The next weight in importance is *exponential*, $\rho^{|S|}$ — the biased noise operator — and the corresponding statement, **hypercontractivity**, is the missing ingredient between this page and the [Kahn–Kalai–Linial theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahn%E2%80%93Kalai%E2%80%93Linial_theorem): every balanced monotone event has a site of influence at least $c\log n/n$. The pleasant part is that hypercontractivity **tensorises**, and tensorisation is nothing but repeated application of the Product Rule from §3, coordinate by coordinate. The only genuinely new ingredient is a two-variable polynomial inequality on a *single* coordinate. The bookkeeping, once set up, keeps paying.
Further reading - [Analysis of Boolean Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10386) — the standard reference for the unbiased theory, influences, and hypercontractivity. - [Percolation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percolation_theory) — the physical setting in which sharp thresholds were first observed. - [Efron–Stein inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efron%E2%80%93Stein_inequality) — the variance bound whose exact defect is computed here. - [Russo's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo%27s_formula) — the derivative of a monotone probability is the total influence.
